Select to Think: Unlocking SLM Potential with Local Sufficiency

Wenxuan Ye Affiliation: TUM School of Computation, Information and Technology, Technical University of Munich Affiliation: Heisenberg Research Center, Huawei Technologies Duesseldorf GmbH Correspondence to: wenxuan.ye@tum.de    Yangyang Zhang Affiliation: Center for Information and Language Processing, Ludwig Maximilian University of Munich    Xueli An Affiliation: Heisenberg Research Center, Huawei Technologies Duesseldorf GmbH    Georg Carle Affiliation: TUM School of Computation, Information and Technology, Technical University of Munich    Yunpu Ma Affiliation: Center for Information and Language Processing, Ludwig Maximilian University of Munich
Abstract

Small language models (SLMs) offer computational efficiency for scalable deployment, yet they often fall short of the reasoning power exhibited by their larger counterparts (LLMs). To mitigate this gap, current approaches invoke an LLM to generate tokens at points of reasoning divergence, but these external calls introduce substantial latency and costs. Alternatively, standard distillation is often hindered by the capacity limitation, as SLMs struggle to accurately mimic the LLM’s complex generative distribution. We address this dilemma by identifying local sufficiency: at divergence points, the LLM’s preferred token consistently resides within the SLM’s top-KK next-token predictions, even when failing to emerge as the SLM top-1 choice. We therefore propose Select to Think (S2T), which reframes the LLM’s role from open-ended generation to selection among the SLM’s proposals, simplifying the supervision signal to discrete candidate rankings. Leveraging this, we introduce S2T-Local, which distills the selection logic into the SLM, empowering it to perform autonomous re-ranking without inference-time LLM dependency. Empirically, we demonstrate that a 1.5B SLM’s top-8 candidates capture the 32B LLM’s choice with 95% hit rate. Translating this potential into performance, S2T-Local improves greedy decoding by 24.1% on average across benchmarks, effectively matching the efficacy of 8-path self-consistency while operating with single-trajectory efficiency.

Keywords: 
Machine Learning, ICML

1 Introduction

Large Language Models (LLMs) demonstrate superior reasoning capabilities, but their high inference costs limit scalable deployment, motivating growing interest in Small Language Models (SLMs) (Schick and Schütze, 2021; Magister et al., 2023; Liu et al., 2024). However, SLMs often underperform on complex multi-step reasoning tasks (Achiam et al., 2023; Yang et al., 2024). To navigate this trade-off, collaborative reasoning has emerged as a promising paradigm, leveraging the LLM to assist the SLM during inference (Shnitzer et al., 2023; Kim et al., 2025; Wang et al., 2025b). Early systems primarily rely on query-level routing or cascades, escalating entire prompts to the LLM based on difficulty (Varshney and Baral, 2022; Chen et al., 2023b; Ong et al., 2025). Yet, recent analyses reveal that errors are predominantly localized, where a small number of critical tokens can cause irreversible drift from the optimal trajectory (Lin et al., 2024; Fu et al., 2025a). This observation has motivated finer-grained collaboration that intervenes selectively at these divergent points, enabling sparse LLM interventions (Huang et al., 2026).

Despite the sparsity of interventions, these approaches remain constrained by latency and computational cost, as each correction necessitates a synchronous LLM call with substantial prefill overhead. Alternatively, attempting to internalize this reasoning capability via standard distillation is hindered by the inherent capacity gap (Li et al., 2025). Forcing the SLM to match the teacher’s distribution over a vast, open-ended vocabulary often compels it to mimic probability peaks that contradict its internal priors, resulting in brittle imitation rather than robust decision rules (Cho and Hariharan, 2019; Chen et al., 2025).

To address this dilemma, we shift focus from generative imitation to the potential of the SLM’s top-KK next-token candidates, raising a key question:

At divergence points, does the SLM’s candidate set suffice to capture the LLM’s preferred choice?

As illustrated in Figure 1, uncovering such local sufficiency implies a fundamental paradigm shift: resource-intensive open-ended LLM generation can be substituted with selection over the SLM’s own proposals. This reformulation fundamentally alters the learning objective, effectively bypassing the capacity gap: instead of demanding exact mimicry of the teacher’s generative peaks, it reduces the challenge to a far simpler goal, identifying the optimal token from a bounded candidate set.

To operationalize this insight, we introduce Select to Think (S2T). Diverging from prior works that primarily study when to intervene, our innovation redefines the intervention mechanism. Specifically, we constrain the LLM to choose from the SLM’s generated options, yielding discrete supervision signals that are inherently easier to distill than complex probability distributions. Capitalizing on these signals, we further propose S2T-Local, which internalizes the selection logic into the SLM itself, creating a teacher-free variant. Since forcing direct probability alignment risks distorting the native distribution, we decouple selection from generation instead. Specifically, adapting the Zero-overhead Inference-time Prediction (ZIP) framework (Manvi et al., 2025), we repurpose the logits of reserved tokens to encode preference scores. This design effectively isolates the selection signal, enabling the SLM to self-evaluate via a learned “inner critic” without perturbing its standard vocabulary statistics.

We systematically evaluate S2T across diverse reasoning benchmarks. First, our analysis validates the local sufficiency: the 1.5B SLM’s top-8 candidates capture the 32B teacher’s preference with a 95% hit rate. This phenomenon proves consistent across model scales (down to 0.5B) and architectures. Second, we confirm the learnability of this signal, where the internalized selector achieves a robust 67% agreement with the LLM on held-out instances. Translating these factors into performance, S2T-Local improves greedy decoding by average of 24.1% at comparable computational cost, effectively matching the performance of 8-path self-consistency with single-trajectory efficiency.

Our contributions are summarized as follows:

  • •

    Insight: We formalize and empirically verify local sufficiency: at divergence points, the preferred token of larger models are consistently contained within the SLM’s top-K predictions. This finding identifies selection refinement, rather than generative imitation, as a pivotal avenue for SLM optimization.

  • •

    Framework: Select to Think (S2T) reframes LLM assistance as explicit selection over SLM proposals, simplifying the distillation objective from complex distribution matching to a tractable ranking task.

  • •

    Method: We introduce S2T-Local, a teacher-free variant that internalizes the selection logic. By utilizing reserved tokens to encode preference scores, we decouple generation from evaluation, enabling the SLM to perform autonomous re-ranking without external overhead.

  • •

    Experiments: Through extensive experiments and mechanistic analysis, we demonstrate that S2T-Local improves greedy decoding by 24.1% on average, effectively matching the performance of 8-path self-consistency with single-trajectory efficiency.

2 Related Works

Model routing. To mitigate LLM inference costs, adaptive strategies dynamically delegate generation tasks based on input difficulty. While early systems routed entire queries (Chen et al., 2023b), more recent works enable fine-grained token-level interventions, dynamically invoking the LLM exclusively for critical tokens  (Fu et al., 2025a; Huang et al., 2026). However, these approaches still rely on LLM generation as the intervention primitive, which requires synchronous teacher calls and injects external tokens into the SLM trajectory.

Speculative decoding. Speculative decoding accelerates inference by employing an efficient drafter to propose tokens and a target LLM to verify (Leviathan et al., 2023; Chen et al., 2023a). Extensions such as SpecInfer (Miao et al., 2023) and SpecTr (Chen et al., 2024) verify trees or cascades to improve acceptance rates. Recent variants (e.g., SpecReason (Pan et al., 2025)) relax strict token matching by verifying reasoning steps semantically. This line primarily targets latency reduction for LLM inference, and typically retains an external verifier model at test time, whereas our goal is to enhance the SLM’s reasoning performance through localized guidance.

Knowledge distillation. Standard distillation often requires matching a strong teacher’s open-ended output distribution, which can be brittle under large LLM-SLM capacity gaps (Wang et al., 2025a; Zhang et al., 2025). Recent work therefore moves toward selective supervision, for example by emphasizing key reasoning tokens or high-value steps, e.g., RLKD (Peng and Zhang, 2025) and TSD-KD (Anonymous, 2026). However, they remain bound to the generative paradigm by optimizing the SLM to match the LLM’s distribution over the full vocabulary.

Test-time compute scaling. A separate line of work improves reasoning by allocating more inference compute, typically via sampling-and-aggregation (Self-Consistency (Wang et al., 2022)) or explicit search (Tree of Thoughts (Yao et al., 2023)). Recent advances attempt to localize this computation through token-level mechanisms, such as selective latent iterations (Think-at-Hard (Fu et al., 2025b)) or parallel branching (Multiplex Thinking (Tang et al., 2026)). However, these methods generally remain rooted in optimizing the generative process, bottlenecked by the model’s inherent capacity constraints.

3 Preliminaries

3.1 Autoregressive decoding

Let 𝒱\mathcal{V} be a token vocabulary. Given an input xx sampled from a data distribution 𝒳\mathcal{X}, an autoregressive model generates a response y=(y1,…,yT)y=(y_{1},\ldots,y_{T}). Let y<t:=(y1,…,yt−1)y_{<t}:=(y_{1},\ldots,y_{t-1}) be the prefix before step tt, and define the decoding state as st:=(x,y<t)s_{t}:=(x,y_{<t}). A language model πθ\pi_{\theta} produces logits zt∈ℝ|𝒱|z_{t}\in\mathbb{R}^{|\mathcal{V}|}, inducing a next-token distribution pθ(⋅∣st)=softmax(zt)p_{\theta}(\cdot\mid s_{t})=\mathrm{softmax}(z_{t}). Standard inference typically employs greedy decoding:

y^t=arg​maxv∈𝒱⁡pθ​(v∣st)\hat{y}_{t}=\operatorname*{arg\,max}_{v\in\mathcal{V}}\,p_{\theta}(v\mid s_{t}) (1)

To model collaborative inference, let πθL\pi_{\theta_{L}} and πθS\pi_{\theta_{S}} denote a large teacher (LLM) and a small student (SLM), parameterized by θL\theta_{L} and θS\theta_{S} respectively. Existing collaborative baselines can be abstracted via a binary trigger variable gt∈{0,1}g_{t}\in\{0,1\} that governs the token source:

y^t={arg​maxv∈𝒱⁡pθS​(v∣st),if ​gt=0,arg​maxv∈𝒱⁡pθL​(v∣st),if ​gt=1.\hat{y}_{t}=\begin{cases}\operatorname*{arg\,max}_{v\in\mathcal{V}}\,p_{\theta_{S}}(v\mid s_{t}),&\text{if }g_{t}=0,\\ \operatorname*{arg\,max}_{v\in\mathcal{V}}\,p_{\theta_{L}}(v\mid s_{t}),&\text{if }g_{t}=1.\end{cases} (2)

For brevity, we present the greedy form, though our formulation generalizes naturally to stochastic sampling. Typically, gtg_{t} is determined by a triggering strategy (e.g., uncertainty thresholding).

3.2 Zero-overhead Inference-time Prediction (ZIP)

Zero-overhead Inference-time Prediction (ZIP) (Manvi et al., 2025) repurposes a set of reserved tokens ℛ⊂𝒱\mathcal{R}\subset\mathcal{V}, and utilizes their logits to encode auxiliary predictions. These tokens are masked from the generative distribution to preserve valid text generation, yet their logits zt​[ℛ]z_{t}[\mathcal{R}] remain available to encode auxiliary signals. ZIP computes a scalar prediction s^t\hat{s}_{t} by applying a readout mapping ψ:ℝ|ℛ|→ℝ\psi:\mathbb{R}^{|\mathcal{R}|}\to\mathbb{R} to these reserved logits (e.g., via a weighted linear projection):

s^t=ψ⁡(zt​[ℛ])\hat{s}_{t}=\psi(z_{t}[\mathcal{R}]) (3)

In this work, we adopt this mechanism to parameterize a lightweight selection score, enabling the model to output a quality score s^t\hat{s}_{t} conditional on its current state.

4 Method: the S2T Framework

We introduce S2T, which reframes the collaborative paradigm by substituting open-ended generation with discrete selection over the SLM’s candidates. This shift simplifies the LLM’s guidance into a manageable scoring task, which can then be distilled into the SLM to enable high-performance local inference without external LLM calls.

We organize the methodology as follows: Section 4.1 briefly outlines the intervention trigger (determining when to intervene). The core of our framework follows: Section 4.2 details the candidate selection protocol (determining what and how to select), and Section 4.3 describes how this selection logic is internalized for fully local inference. Finally, Section 4.4 analyzes the theoretical advantages of this paradigm.

4.1 Intervention trigger

To balance reasoning accuracy with efficiency, we first define an oracle trigger to identify critical decoding steps. Following prior findings that reasoning errors often stem from a few pivotal tokens (Lin et al., 2024), we utilize the KL divergence DKL(pθL∥pθS)D_{\text{KL}}(p_{\theta_{L}}\|p_{\theta_{S}}) as the metric for disagreement. The binary trigger gtg_{t} is activated (gt=1g_{t}=1) if the divergence exceeds the top-τ\tau-th percentile observed in the calibration set. To enable local inference, we distill this oracle decision into a lightweight predictor. Given that the trigger module is largely orthogonal to our selection mechanism and has been explored in prior studies (Fu et al., 2025a; Huang et al., 2026), we prioritize our discussion on the selection logic and defer the implementation details of the trigger head to Appendix E.

4.2 Selection mechanism

When the trigger activates, S2T replaces standard SLM decoding with candidate-based selection. First, the SLM constructs a local candidate set 𝒞t\mathcal{C}_{t} by identifying the top-KK tokens from its next-token distribution (or sampling via multinomial). The decoding step then becomes a maximization over this constrained set, governed by a scoring function 𝒮⁡(c,st)\mathcal{S}(c;s_{t}):

y^t=arg​maxc∈𝒞t⁡𝒮​(c,st)\hat{y}_{t}=\operatorname*{arg\,max}_{c\in\mathcal{C}_{t}}\>\mathcal{S}(c;s_{t}) (4)

By restricting to student proposals, the choice remains within the student’s local support and reduces the LLM’s decision space to KK candidates.

We instantiate the scoring function 𝒮⁡(⋅)\mathcal{S}(\cdot) in two settings, with the algorithmic flow of S2T in Algorithm 1 (Appendix A).

S2T. A collaborative framework where the LLM actively scores the SLM’s proposals. The score is defined as the LLM’s conditional probability for each candidate: 𝒮⁡(c,st)=pθL​(c∣st)\mathcal{S}(c;s_{t})=p_{\theta_{L}}(c\mid s_{t}). Here, the LLM provides a restricted supervision signal via ranking the student’s proposals, rather than generating open-ended text.

S2T-Local. To remove inference-time dependencies on the LLM, we introduce S2T-Local, a variant that replaces the LLM with a distilled internal selector. Concretely, for each candidate c∈𝒞tc\in\mathcal{C}_{t}, we construct the augmented state stc:=(x,y<t⊕c)s_{t}^{\,c}:=(x,y_{<t}\oplus c). We then perform a forward pass on stcs_{t}^{\,c} to extract the logits zθS​[ℛ]z_{\theta_{S}}[\mathcal{R}] corresponding to the reserved set ℛ\mathcal{R}. Following the discrete binning approach, the preference score is computed as:

𝒮l​o​c​a​l​(c,st)=𝐯⊤​softmax​(zθS​(stc)​[ℛ])\mathcal{S}_{local}(c;s_{t})=\mathbf{v}^{\top}\mathrm{softmax}\left(z_{\theta_{S}}(s_{t}^{\,c})[\mathcal{R}]\right) (5)

where 𝐯\mathbf{v} is a vector of predefined bin values. In practice, we maximize efficiency by batching the KK augmented inputs {stc}c∈𝒞t\{s_{t}^{\,c}\}_{c\in\mathcal{C}_{t}} to compute all candidate scores in a single parallel forward pass. Finally, we append the highest-scoring candidate to the prefix and continue decoding from the updated state.

4.3 Distillation of the selection logic

Data Collection. We construct a training dataset 𝒳\mathcal{X} by rolling out the SLM. At each intervention step, we generate the local candidate set 𝒞t\mathcal{C}_{t} from the student’s next-token distribution pθS(⋅∣st)p_{\theta_{S}}(\cdot\mid s_{t}). The teacher then annotates these candidates by evaluating their next-token likelihood under the same prefix sts_{t}: pθL​(c∣st)p_{\theta_{L}}(c\mid s_{t}) for each c∈𝒞tc\in\mathcal{C}_{t}. The optimal candidate c⋆c^{\star} is then identified as the one with the highest likelihood among the set.

Optimization objective. We jointly minimize a selection loss and a stability regularizer:

ℒ⁡(θS)=ℒsel+β⋅ℒreg\mathcal{L}(\theta_{S})=\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{sel}}+\beta\cdot\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{reg}} (6)

The selection term ℒsel\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{sel}} maximizes the likelihood of the target candidate c⋆c^{\star} over the set 𝒞t\mathcal{C}_{t}. We formulate this as a cross-entropy loss over the scores predicted by the student:

ℒsel=−log⁡exp⁡(𝒮local​(c⋆,st)/T)∑c′∈𝒞texp⁡(𝒮local​(c′,st)/T)\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{sel}}=-\log\frac{\exp\left(\mathcal{S}_{\text{local}}(c^{\star};s_{t})/T\right)}{\sum_{c^{\prime}\in\mathcal{C}_{t}}\exp\left(\mathcal{S}_{\text{local}}(c^{\prime};s_{t})/T\right)} (7)

where TT is a temperature hyperparameter controlling the sharpness of the distribution. Minimizing this term increases the discriminative margin between the target c⋆c^{\star} and other candidates, effectively aligning the reserved-token readout to correctly capture the teacher’s preference.

To prevent the fine-tuning from distorting the model’s general linguistic capabilities, we enforce a stability constraint ℒreg\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{reg}}. We calculate the KL divergence between the fine-tuned distribution πθS\pi_{\theta_{S}} and the frozen base model πS,base\pi_{S,\text{base}} over the standard text vocabulary 𝒱text=𝒱∖ℛ\mathcal{V}_{\text{text}}=\mathcal{V}\setminus\mathcal{R}:

ℒreg=𝔻KL(πS,base(⋅∣st)∥πθS(⋅∣st))𝒱text\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{reg}}=\mathbb{D}_{\text{KL}}\big(\pi_{S,\text{base}}(\cdot\mid s_{t})\,\big\|\,\pi_{\theta_{S}}(\cdot\mid s_{t})\big)_{\mathcal{V}_{\text{text}}} (8)

This ensures that while the reserved tokens ℛ\mathcal{R} learn to carry discriminative signals, the standard tokens continue to function as a coherent language model.

4.4 Analysis of the collaborative selection mechanism

Following standard formulations in imitation learning (Ross et al., 2011; Sutton et al., 1998), we view autoregressive decoding as a horizon-TT sequential decision process. Given parameters θ\theta, the decoder induces a decision rule fθ:𝒳×𝒱⋆→𝒱f_{\theta}:\mathcal{X}\times\mathcal{V}^{\star}\to\mathcal{V}, where 𝒱⋆=⋃n=0∞𝒱n\mathcal{V}^{\star}=\bigcup_{n=0}^{\infty}\mathcal{V}^{n} denotes the set of all possible prefixes, and fθf_{\theta} represents the decoding mechanism.

In S2T framework, the decoder first determines a dynamic candidate size ktk_{t} based on the trigger gt​(st)∈{0,1}g_{t}(s_{t})\in\{0,1\}:

kt=K​if​gt​(st)=1​else​  1k_{t}=K\>\>\text{if}\>\>g_{t}(s_{t})=1\>\>\text{else}\>\>1 (9)

The search space is then constrained to a local candidate set 𝒞t\mathcal{C}_{t} comprising the ktk_{t} tokens from the SLM’s probability distribution. Finally, the decision rule fθf_{\theta} selects the next token via the scoring function 𝒮\mathcal{S}, as in Equation 4. This unified formulation recovers standard decoding as a special case: when gt=0g_{t}=0, the set 𝒞t\mathcal{C}_{t} collapses to a single token, forcing fθf_{\theta} to follow the SLM’s original path regardless of the scoring function.

We assume access to a teacher reference model that induces an optimal reference token y⋆​(st)∈𝒱y^{\star}(s_{t})\in\mathcal{V} at each step (e.g., y⋆​(st)=arg​maxv∈𝒱⁡pθL​(v∣st)y^{\star}(s_{t})=\operatorname*{arg\,max}_{v\in\mathcal{V}}p_{\theta_{L}}(v\mid s_{t})). We measure the instantaneous 0-1 decoding error as:

ℓ(st,y^t):=𝕀[y^t≠y⋆(st)]∈{0,1}\ell(s_{t},\hat{y}_{t})\;:=\;\mathbb{I}[\hat{y}_{t}\neq y^{\star}(s_{t})]\in\{0,1\} (10)

Consequently, for any state sts_{t}, the error can be decomposed into two distinct sources:

𝕀[fθ(st)≠y⋆(st)]=\displaystyle\mathbb{I}[f_{\theta}(s_{t})\neq y^{\star}(s_{t})]\;= 𝕀[y⋆(st)∉𝒞t]⏟δhit(t)​(kt,st)\displaystyle\underbrace{\mathbb{I}[y^{\star}(s_{t})\notin\mathcal{C}_{t}]}_{\textstyle\delta_{\text{hit}}^{(t)}(k_{t};s_{t})} (11)
+\displaystyle\;+ 𝕀⁡[y⋆​(st)∈𝒞t,fθ​(st)≠y⋆​(st)]⏟δsel(t)​(kt,st)\displaystyle\underbrace{\mathbb{I}[y^{\star}(s_{t})\in\mathcal{C}_{t},\,f_{\theta}(s_{t})\neq y^{\star}(s_{t})]}_{\textstyle\delta_{\text{sel}}^{(t)}(k_{t};s_{t})}

where δhit\delta_{\text{hit}} and δsel\delta_{\text{sel}} denote the hit failure and selection failure, respectively.

Proposition.

Let dθtd_{\theta}^{t} denote the state distribution at step tt induced by rolling out fθf_{\theta}. For any model θ\theta and candidate size KK, the cumulative error decomposes as

ℰ⁡(θ)\displaystyle\mathcal{E}(\theta) =∑t=1T𝔼st∼dθt​[ℓ⁡(st,fθ​(st))]\displaystyle=\sum_{t=1}^{T}\mathbb{E}_{s_{t}\sim d_{\theta}^{t}}\Big[\ell(s_{t},f_{\theta}(s_{t}))\Big] (12)
=∑t=1T𝔼st∼dθt[(1−gt(st))⋅δhit(t)(1;st)+\displaystyle=\sum_{t=1}^{T}\mathbb{E}_{s_{t}\sim d_{\theta}^{t}}\bigg[(1-g_{t}(s_{t}))\cdot\delta_{\text{hit}}^{(t)}(1;s_{t})\>+
gt(st)⋅(δhit(t)(K;st)+δsel(t)(K;st))]\displaystyle g_{t}(s_{t})\cdot\bigg(\delta_{\text{hit}}^{(t)}(K;s_{t})+\delta_{\text{sel}}^{(t)}(K;s_{t})\bigg)\bigg]

This proposition formalizes the trade-off between search coverage and selection precision. While increasing KK reduces hit failure (δhit\delta_{\text{hit}}) by expanding the search space, it introduces selection error (δsel\delta_{\text{sel}}) due to increased discriminative difficulty. S2T reduces cumulative error by balancing increased candidate coverage (lower δhit\delta_{\text{hit}} at moderate KK) against minimal selection difficulty (δsel\delta_{\text{sel}}).

5 Experiments

To empirically validate S2T, we conduct a comprehensive evaluation designed to answer four research questions:

  • •

    RQ1 (Overall performance): How does S2T compare to LLM-free and collaborative baselines?

  • •

    RQ2 (Paradigm validity): Does the local sufficiency hypothesis hold, and can the selection paradigm recover the performance of open-ended generation?

  • •

    RQ3 (Distillation efficacy): Can the SLM effectively internalize teacher preferences to enable autonomous scoring mechanism?

  • •

    RQ4 (Ablation): How do key design choices impact the overall performance?

5.1 Setup

We outline key configurations below, with full implementation details provided in Appendix B.

Models and Datasets. We utilize the Qwen2.5-Instruct family (Qwen, 2025), pairing 0.5B and 1.5B students with a 32B teacher to simulate realistic capacity gaps. We evaluate on mathematical reasoning (GSM8K (Cobbe et al., 2021), MATH (Lightman et al., 2023), OlympiadBench (He et al., 2024), AIME25 (Zhang and Math-AI, 2025)), coding (HumanEval (Chen et al., 2021)), and broad knowledge (MMLU-Pro (Wang et al., 2024)). We adopt a zero-shot protocol with a task-specific system instruction.

S2T Configurations. Using KL divergence as the intervention signal, S2T directs the SLM to sample KK candidates via multinomial and LLM to rank. To enable local inference, we distill this ranking logic into the SLM. Coupled with a learned gating mechanism to trigger intervention, S2T-Local empowers the SLM to achieve fully autonomous inference without external LLM calls. Unless otherwise specified, we set the candidate size K=8K=8 and the intervention budget to τ=1%\tau=1\%. Results are reported as average metrics per instance, across three random seeds to ensure statistical robustness.

Baselines. We categorize baselines by their reliance on external LLMs during inference. SLM-only methods operate independently, including SLM Greedy, the standard distillation baseline DistilQwen2.5 (Wang et al., 2025a), and TSD-KD (Anonymous, 2026), which applies distillation exclusively to critical tokens. We also include test-time scaling strategies: Self-Consistency (Maj@8) (Wang et al., 2022) for ensemble sampling, Multiplex-Thinking (Mul-T) (Tang et al., 2026) via soft token aggregation, and Think-at-Hard (TaH) (Fu et al., 2025b) for dynamic budget allocation. Collaborative methods include generative collaboration frameworks like SpecReason (SpecR) (Pan et al., 2025) and R2R (Fu et al., 2025a). Moreover, to isolate the benefit of selection versus generation, we implement Takeover, a controlled baseline that uses the same trigger schedule and budget as S2T but instructs the LLM to generate the next token rather than perform selection.

Training Details. To rigorously evaluate out-of-distribution (OOD) generalization, we train S2T exclusively on the MATH training split, leaving all other benchmarks entirely unseen. We curate a dataset of 2k trajectories by selecting the top τ=10%\tau=10\% instances of KL divergence, with K=16K=16 candidates per step annotated by the teacher. For optimization, we apply LoRA adapters on attention and MLP modules, while additionally unfreezing the specific lmhead\text{lm}_{\text{head}} embeddings for the reserved tokens ℛ\mathcal{R}, with |ℛ|=16|\mathcal{R}|=16. This configuration yields highly efficient adaptation: 35.7M and 74.3M trainable parameters for the 0.5B and 1.5B models, respectively (<6%<6\% of total capacity).

Metric. Hit rate (Hit@KK) measures the probability that the LLM’s preferred token is included within the SLM’s top-KK candidate set, complementary to δhit\delta_{\mathrm{hit}}. Agree@1 denotes the probability that the distilled selector successfully identifies the LLM’s choice from the candidates.

5.2 RQ1: Overall performance

Table 1 presents a comprehensive evaluation across two model scales (0.5B and 1.5B) on six diverse benchmarks.

RQ1.1: How effective is S2T-Local in math reasoning? It achieves significant improvements compared to both distillation baselines and recent adaptive strategies grounded in non-uniform compute allocation for “hard” tokens. We observe an average improvement of 24.1% on the 1.5B model, which amplifies to a remarkable 38% gain on the smaller 0.5B scale. Remarkably, the single-trajectory S2T-Local matches Self-consistency (Maj@8) with about 1/81/8 of the compute cost.

This performance leap is fundamentally rooted in the high hit rate across model scales. As demonstrated in our subsequent analysis, while the 1.5B model achieves a Hit@8 of 95%, even the smaller 0.5B SLM reaches a striking 83%. This suggests that the optimal reasoning path often resides within the model’s top-KK proposals; by effectively exploiting this hidden information, S2T-Local converts this untapped potential into substantial performance gains.

RQ1.2: How generalizable is S2T-Local? Beyond math tasks, S2T-Local demonstrates exceptional transferability to diverse domains, including code generation (HumanEval) and complex general reasoning (MMLU-Pro). As shown in Table 1, we observe consistent performance gains across these benchmarks, confirming that the learned selection mechanism captures universal reasoning preferences rather than relying on domain-specific heuristics.

RQ1.3: How effective is selection-based guidance in collaborative settings? In the collaborative setting, S2T is consistently comparable to strong collaborative methods across diverse benchmarks, as demonstrated in Table 1. In addition, we evaluate collaboration performance by varying the candidate size (KK) and the intervention rate (τ\tau). Figure 2a shows consistent gains with increasing KK or τ\tau, quickly saturating at larger budgets. Crucially, selection-based guidance (K≥8K\geq 8) matches the generative baseline, demonstrating that discriminative selection is sufficient to recover LLM reasoning without the need for expensive generation. (See Table A1 for results on additional benchmarks.)

5.3 RQ2: Paradigm validity

A core hypothesis underlying S2T is that the SLM retains the underlying capacity to match the LLM’s reasoning, yet this ability is often masked by the sub-optimality of standard decoding strategies. In this section, we empirically validate this premise. For the following analysis, we default to the 1.5B SLM and MATH500, unless noted otherwise.

RQ2.1: Does the candidate set cover the token preferred by LLM? In Figure 2b, fixing the intervention frequency at τ=1%\tau=1\% and varying candidate size KK, we observe that both hit rate and downstream accuracy rise rapidly and quickly saturate, exhibiting diminishing returns beyond small values of K=8K=8. Conversely, with fixed K=8K=8 (Figure 2c), the hit rate remains stable, while accuracy improves as higher τ\tau enables more frequent refinements.

Validation of Local Sufficiency. We visualize the candidate hit rate in Figure 3. While greedy decoding (Hit@1) aligns with the LLM only 30%30\% of the time, expanding to a modest K=8K=8 captures the target token in over 95% of cases. This empirical evidence confirms that the LLM’s preferred tokens almost always lie within the SLM’s local distribution. Consequently, failures at critical steps stem not from an absence of candidates, but from an inability to prioritize the available candidates.

Generalization. We further substantiate this observation across the 0.5B scale, the Gemma architecture, and general reasoning tasks (see Figure A1, Figure A2). Surprisingly, the 0.5B SLM achieves a Hit@8 exceeding 83%, despite its significantly smaller parameter count. The consistent high coverage across different scales and domains confirms that local sufficiency is an inherent characteristic, providing a robust foundation for selection-based inference.

RQ2.2: How does the selection mechanism utilize this potential? In Figure 4(a), lower thresholds maximize probability divergence, suggesting that S2T prioritizes tokens where SLM uncertainty contrasts most sharply with teacher preference. As visualized in Figure 4(b), the top-left concentration highlights the mechanism’s ability to recover LLM-endorsed tokens from the candidate set, even when they are severely underestimated by greedy decoding. By leveraging the LLM’s superior performance to minimize selection error, S2T effectively capitalizes on the high inherent hit rate, successfully translating this potential into superior task accuracy as analyzed in Section 4.4.

RQ2.3: How does hit rate evolve as the candidate set size KK increases? The rank CDFs across various tasks (Figure A3) consistently exhibit a steep initial surge in Hit@KK. While the baseline accuracy varies, we observe a universal saturation point around K=8K=8, beyond which marginal gains rapidly diminish.

5.4 RQ3: Distillation efficacy

RQ3.1: How accurately does the distilled selector replicate the teacher’s preferences? As shown in Table 2, the selector achieves a robust Agree@1 of 68%. This high alignment proves that the student has successfully internalized the teacher’s judgment, directly driving the performance gains observed in Table 1. In addition, confidence statistics reveal a similar corrective dynamic as in Figure 4: the selector typically rescues tokens with low SLM probability but high LLM certainty, effectively recovering valid reasoning paths that were underestimated by the greedy decoding. To further examine the alignment between predicted scores and teacher ranks, we present Figure A5, which reveals a sharp “winner-takes-all” characteristic where the selector decisively isolates the top candidate while suppressing sub-optimal ones.

RQ3.2: Can the selection capability generalize to OOD tasks? Remarkably, despite being trained exclusively on the MATH dataset, the distilled selector demonstrates robust generalization, achieving high accuracy across OOD benchmarks, as shown in Table 1. For a comprehensive analysis across 0.5B models and additional tasks, please refer to Table A2 in the Appendix.

RQ3.3: What is the computational overhead of S2T-Local? The inference process augments standard SLM decoding with a lightweight projection for trigger evaluation. Upon triggering, the SLM generates and scores the candidate set 𝒞t\mathcal{C}_{t}; thus, the additional computational cost is dominated by these sparse interventions. As quantified by the average token count and wall-clock time in Table 3, S2T achieves substantial speedups, validating its efficiency against intensive baselines. Detailed comparisons are provided in Table A3 and Table A4.

5.5 RQ4: Ablation

RQ4.1: Is the effectiveness of S2T dependent on specific trigger metrics? Ablation studies across various trigger metrics verify that our framework is invariant to the specific choice of trigger. As evidenced in Table A5, S2T consistently matches the generative baseline regardless of the underlying trigger criterion.

RQ4.2: How does candidate generation strategy impact ranking efficacy? As shown in Table A6, common sampling parameters (e.g., top-p=0.7p=0.7) truncates the probability tail, leading to |𝒞t|≈1.5|\mathcal{C}_{t}|\approx 1.5 that prematurely excludes LLM-preferred tokens and caps accuracy. Conversely, S2T restores search diversity via unrestricted sampling (K=8K=8), boosting accuracy to 81.1%.

RQ4.3: What are the key training strategies for an effective distilled selector? To justify our design choices, we evaluated alternative strategies, including head-only tuning and mimicking LLM’s scores on the candidates. We find that head-only updates provide insufficient expressive capacity, while matching the LLM’s scores overwhelms the student’s reserved logit space with excessive noise. Consequently, we fine-tune SLM via a discrete selection loss, with a comprehensive analysis of these training phases provided in Appendix D.4.

6 Conclusion

In this work, we argue that the primary reasoning bottleneck in SLMs is not a lack of generation potential, but a misalignment in candidate ranking. Our investigation into local sufficiency reveals that SLMs often generate viable next tokens within their top-candidate set, yet superior options can be suppressed by a suboptimal internal ranking. Leveraging it, S2T reframes distillation from open-ended distribution matching to discriminative selection over a bounded support, providing a more efficient path to unlocking the model’s inherent potential. Specifically, our distilled SLM yields a 24.1% accuracy gain, achieving performance comparable to 8-path self-consistency while operating in a single-trajectory, teacher-free manner. Beyond these empirical gains, S2T recasts the SLM as an active selector of its own proposals rather than a passive imitator, suggesting a path toward resource-efficient scaling.

Impact Statement

This paper introduces a selection-based distillation framework to enhance the reasoning of small language models. Our work contributes to the development of resource-efficient AI systems, enabling capable reasoning on edge devices with significantly lower latency and energy costs compared to traditional collaborative and ensemble methods.

This appendix is organized to provide comprehensive methodological specifics and supplementary evidence. We begin by detailing the formal inference algorithm in Appendix A, followed by a thorough description of our evaluation setup in Appendix B. Appendix C offers an extended discussion of related works to further contextualize S2T within the broader literature. Technical depth regarding the distillation of the selector and the training protocols for the trigger head is provided in Appendices D and E, respectively. Finally, Appendix F presents additional experimental results to further substantiate the robustness of our framework.

Appendix A Inference Algorithm

Algorithm 1 formalizes the S2T inference procedure, detailing the transition from standard generation to targeted discriminative selection at critical reasoning steps.

Appendix B Evaluation Details

B.1 Benchmark

Mathematical reasoning benchmarks.

  • •

    GSM8K (Cobbe et al., 2021): A dataset of 8,500 linguistically diverse grade school math word problems requiring 2-8 step reasoning, serving as a standard benchmark for evaluating basic mathematical reasoning capabilities.

  • •

    MATH-500 (Lightman et al., 2023): A subset of 500 challenging competition-level mathematics problems sampled from the MATH dataset, covering seven mathematical domains (algebra, geometry, number theory, etc.) ranging from AMC 8 to IMO difficulty levels.

  • •

    AIME (Zhang and Math-AI, 2025): American Invitational Mathematics Examination problems, featuring high-difficulty competition mathematics that requires advanced problem-solving skills and multi-step reasoning.

  • •

    OlympiadBench (He et al., 2024): A bilingual (English and Chinese) competition-level benchmark containing challenging problems from mathematical and scientific olympiads, testing advanced reasoning and problem-solving abilities.

Comprehensive reasoning benchmarks. MMLU-Pro (Wang et al., 2024): An enhanced version of MMLU (Massive Multitask Language Understanding) with more challenging questions across 14 domains including mathematics, physics, computer science, and humanities, designed to reduce sensitivity to prompt variations and better assess reasoning capabilities.

Code generation benchmark. HumanEval (Chen et al., 2021): A benchmark of 164 hand-written programming problems for evaluating functional correctness of code synthesis, each consisting of a function signature, docstring, body, and unit tests.

We evaluate our models on a diverse set of reasoning benchmarks using a standardized zero-shot Chain-of-Thought (CoT) protocol. For mathematical datasets, we follow the evaluation protocol of Qwen2.5-Math (Yang et al., 2024). We extract the final answer (typically enclosed in boxed format) and compute Exact Match (EM) accuracy after standardizing formats using their official normalization scripts.

For HumanEval, we employ the pass@1 metric using the official evaluation framework from OpenAI’s human-eval repository11 1 https://github.com/openai/human-eval. We format each problem prompt using the model’s chat template with a system message instructing code-only output without markdown formatting or explanations. Code completions are generated with greedy decoding (temperature=0) and a maximum of 512 new tokens. We extract Python code from model outputs using regex patterns to remove markdown code blocks and truncate at subsequent function/class definitions. Functional correctness is verified by executing the generated code against provided unit tests in an isolated environment with a 3-second timeout per test case.

B.2 Prompt

Appendix C Extended Related Work

C.1 Inference-time verification and reranking.

A dominant paradigm for enhancing inference accuracy involves sampling multiple candidates (e.g., Best-of-NN) and reranking them using external signals, such as outcome verifiers (Cobbe et al., 2021), process reward models (PRMs) (Lightman et al., 2023), or LLM-as-a-Judge (Zheng et al., 2023). While effective, these methods typically incur high latency due to extensive sampling and heavy scoring loops. Self-certainty (Kang et al., 2025) leverages the intrinsic probability distribution of LM outputs to estimate response quality without external reward models. However, as documented in the original study, self-certainty-driven Best-of-N selection is less effective than self-consistency on mathematical tasks with the same sampling budget (NN). Consequently, we adopt self-consistency as one representative baseline.

Unlike traditional verifiers that rerank complete solutions, S2T distills teacher logic into a token-level selector, enabling real-time trajectory correction within a single forward pass, bypassing the computational overhead of generating and scoring multiple sequences.

C.2 Contrastive decoding

A parallel line of research steers generation by modifying the decoding distribution itself, rather than employing external search. Foundational contrastive decoding formulations (Li et al., 2023) reshape logits by subtracting an “amateur” (or counterfactual) signal from an “expert” one to suppress generic or hallucinated tokens. This paradigm has inspired various extensions, including context-aware variants to resolve evidence-parametric conflicts (Shi et al., 2024), and internal-contrast methods (e.g., DoLa (Chuang et al., 2023)) that utilize intra-model signals to boost factuality.

Unlike methods that perform heuristic logit surgery across the full vocabulary, S2T operates on selection under bounded support. By explicitly ranking a restricted set of student-proposed candidates, we shift from passive distribution shaping to active path recovery.

Appendix D Implementation on Distilling Selector

D.1 Training data sampling

To facilitate the internalization of the teacher’s discriminatory capability, we construct a preference dataset derived exclusively from the training split of the MATH dataset. We perform data collection by rolling out the SLM. We align the SLM’s internal ranking preferences with the teacher’s probability landscape using a dataset of 2k instances, collected by targeting the top τ=10%\tau=10\% of steps with the highest KL divergence; for each step, we sample K=16K=16 candidates annotated with the LLM’s conditional probabilities.

D.2 Training configurations

The training employs a parameter-efficient fine-tuning (PEFT) strategy where we freeze the pre-trained backbone and inject Low-Rank Adaptation (LoRA) adapters into all linear projections within the attention and feed-forward blocks (specifically targeting the qproj\text{q}_{\text{proj}}, kproj\text{k}_{\text{proj}}, vproj\text{v}_{\text{proj}}, oproj\text{o}_{\text{proj}}, gateproj\text{gate}_{\text{proj}}, upproj\text{up}_{\text{proj}}, and downproj\text{down}_{\text{proj}} modules). We configure the adapters with a rank of r=16r=16, a scaling factor α=32\alpha=32, and a dropout rate of 0.10.1, training for 2 epochs. Crucially, to enable the model to learn the specific semantics of the reserved scoring bins (ℛ\mathcal{R}), we additionally unfreeze the specific lmhead\text{lm}_{\text{head}} embeddings for the reserved tokens ℛ\mathcal{R}, with |ℛ|=16|\mathcal{R}|=16. We utilize a contiguous block of 16 reserved tokens starting from ID 151920 - 151935. This ensures that repurposing their logits does not interfere with the model’s linguistic capabilities. This configuration yields highly efficient adaptation: 35.7M and 74.3M trainable parameters for the 0.5B and 1.5B models, respectively (<6%<6\% of total capacity). The model is optimized using AdamW with a global batch size of 64. We employ a cosine decay learning rate schedule starting from 10−410^{-4}, preceded by a 3% linear warmup phase.

D.3 Training objective function

The model is trained to minimize a composite objective comprising the ranking loss, a stability regularizer, and an auxiliary margin loss. While Eq. (7) (Softmax Cross-Entropy) optimizes global alignment, we find that enforcing a strict separation between the best candidate and its “hard negatives” improves discrimination. We introduce an adaptive pairwise margin loss:

ℒmargin=ReLU⁡(meff−(s⁡(c⋆)−s⁡(cneg)))\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{margin}}\;=\;\mathrm{ReLU}\Big(m_{\mathrm{eff}}-\big(s(c^{\star})-s(c^{\mathrm{neg}})\big)\Big) (13)

where cnegc^{\mathrm{neg}} is the highest-scoring incorrect candidate (hard negative). Notably, we scale the margin dynamically based on the statistical dispersion of the candidate scores to avoid over-penalizing flat distributions. The effective margin is defined as:

meff=σtTm_{\mathrm{eff}}\;=\;\frac{\sigma_{t}}{T} (14)

where σt\sigma_{t} is the standard deviation of scores in the current batch, and T=0.2T=0.2 is the sampling temperature. The final loss is computed as ℒ=ℒsel+ℒmargin+β​ℒKL\mathcal{L}=\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{sel}}+\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{margin}}+\beta\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{KL}}.

Empirically, the KL divergence term contributes a negligible fraction to the total loss, as the updated policy remains in close proximity to the reference model. To ensure effective regularization, we employ a substantial scaling coefficient β\beta, typically parameterized within the range of 1010-100100.

D.4 Detailed analysis of the training evolution

The training of the S2T selector was not a straightforward optimization but a multi-phase refinement process. We categorize the evolution into three distinct phases, each addressing a specific bottleneck in small-model distillation.

Attempt I: initial failure modes. Our initial attempts focused on a naive pointwise classification objective (predicting candidate correctness) using standard linear head-tuning. This approach failed due to two primary reasons: 1) Class imbalance: Because correct candidates are sparse in the student’s proposals, the model optimized for the majority class (incorrect), resulting in a stagnant Agree@1 of ≈25%\approx 25\%. 2) Vocabulary interference: The standard vocabulary embeddings lacked sufficient capacity to simultaneously support generation and discrimination, causing logit drift and linguistic instability.

Attempt II: from distribution mimicry to decisive selection. To overcome Phase I, we transitioned to fine-tuning SLM via LoRA, attempting to match the teacher’s scores of candidates (i.e., learning the full ranking distribution via ListMLE). However, we observed that SLMs lack the capacity to internalize the teacher’s full knowledge. Mimicking the teacher’s “uncertainty” (soft-labels) resulted in a flat logit distribution, where the student could not confidently distinguish the top candidate from the runners-up. For capacity-constrained models, discrete selection (Top-1 Cross-Entropy) is superior. By focusing exclusively on the teacher’s preferred choice, the student develops the sharp decision boundaries necessary for effective filtering.

Attempt III: denoising and structural decoupling. The final breakthrough involved stabilizing the training via teacher margin filtering: We discovered that not all teacher signals are beneficial. When the teacher exhibits low confidence (indicated by a narrow margin between Top-1 and Top-2 scores), its labels serve as noise rather than signal. By enforcing a margin threshold (δ=0.08\delta=0.08), we filter for decisive teacher states, ensuring the student learns from high-quality supervision and significantly boosting Agree@1.

Appendix E Trigger head

To enable learned triggering mechanisms that avoid the computational overhead of always computing KL divergence between SLM and LLM distributions, we train a lightweight header router that predicts critical decoding steps directly from the SLM’s hidden states. The router consists of a criticality prediction head implemented as a two-layer MLP with ReLU activation and dropout (rate 0.1), mapping the SLM’s hidden dimension to a scalar logit. Specifically, the architecture comprises: Linear​(H→256)→ReLU→Dropout​(0.1)→Linear​(256→1)\text{Linear}(H\rightarrow 256)\rightarrow\text{ReLU}\rightarrow\text{Dropout}(0.1)\rightarrow\text{Linear}(256\rightarrow 1), where HH denotes the hidden dimension.

Training data collection. We collect training samples by performing SLM rollouts with KL-based triggering as the oracle signal. At each decoding step, we compute the KL divergence DKL(pθL∥pθS)D_{\text{KL}}(p_{\theta_{L}}\|p_{\theta_{S}}), and label the step as positive (gt=1g_{t}=1) if DKL>Top-​τ​ ThresholdD_{\text{KL}}>\text{Top-}\tau\text{ Threshold} and negative (gt=0g_{t}=0) otherwise. For each step, we store the SLM’s final-layer hidden state (dimension 1536 for Qwen2.5-1.5B-Instruct) along with its binary trigger label. The collected dataset exhibits significant class imbalance, with approximately 20% positive samples (426,406 raw samples yielding 79,895 after downsampling with pos=15,979 and neg=63,916).

Training configuration. To address class imbalance, we employ Binary Cross-Entropy loss with positive class weighting: pos_weight=nnegnpos=4.0\text{pos\_weight}=\frac{n_{\text{neg}}}{n_{\text{pos}}}=4.0. The router is trained for 50 epochs using AdamW optimizer. We split the collected samples into 90% training and 10% validation sets with a fixed random seed (42) to ensure reproducibility. The best checkpoint is selected based on validation accuracy, achieving 87.78% validation accuracy at epoch 36. During inference, we apply a sigmoid activation to the criticality logit and threshold at 0.7 (configurable) to make binary triggering decisions, eliminating the need to compute expensive cross-model KL divergence at every step.

Appendix F Additional Experimental Results

F.1 Extensive analysis on the S2T performance compared to LLM Takeover

The results in Table A1 demonstrate that S2T performs competitively with the generative LLM-takeover baseline across all budgets, with performance parity or slight advantages depending on the candidate size k. This trend is robust across the entire spectrum of intervention budgets (τ\tau), suggesting that selection is a highly effective alternative to full-trajectory decoding even under stringent resource constraints.

Furthermore, we observe a clear scaling relationship between performance and the candidate set size (KK). While a narrow candidate set often bottlenecks the teacher’s corrective capacity, increasing KK consistently elevates accuracy by providing the selector with a more diverse range of alternatives to evaluate. This gain is particularly pronounced in complex reasoning tasks, where a larger K allows the teacher to identify correct tokens that the student ranked too low (e.g., beyond top-4) under greedy decoding. Across all budgets, S2T exhibits a convergence toward or beyond the generative ceiling as KK increases, establishing it as a scalable and computationally efficient framework for teacher-guided reasoning.

F.2 Validity of local sufficiency

To further verify the robustness of the “Local Sufficiency” hypothesis, we extended our radial visualization analysis to a much smaller scale (Qwen2.5-0.5B-Instruct) and a distinct model family (Gemma-2-2B-IT, Gemma-2-27B-IT (Team et al., 2024)). As illustrated in Figure A1 and Figure A2, a striking consistency emerges: despite the significant disparity in model parameters and architectural designs (e.g., different tokenizers and training recipes), the dense central clustering remains invariant. In over 80% of instances across all tested benchmarks, the LLM-preferred tokens consistently reside within the SLM’s top-8 candidate set.

As illustrated in Figure A3, we conduct a fine-grained analysis of the rank distribution of LLM-preferred tokens within the SLM’s logit distribution. A critical observation is the dramatic surge in coverage when expanding the candidate set from K=1K=1 to K=8K=8. Specifically, in the most challenging scenarios where the SLM’s greedy hit rate (Hit@1) falls to a mere 14.1%, the inclusion of just 7 additional candidates (up to K=8K=8) successfully recovers the LLM’s target in 83.2% of cases. This 69.1% absolute gain in the “worst-case” scenario, coupled with the 96.3% peak coverage in other tasks, demonstrates that the bottleneck of SLMs is not a fundamental lack of knowledge, but a systematic selection failure during decoding. Furthermore, this pattern remains remarkably consistent across both the 0.5B and 1.5B scales, suggesting that Local Sufficiency is an intrinsic property of the SLM’s token distribution that persists regardless of model capacity or task difficulty.

We the rank distribution of selected tokens within the SLM’s prediction space in Figure A4. The CDF plot reveals a critical insight: the correct tokens are not absent, but hidden within the immediate search scope. While the SLM often fails to assign the highest probability to the optimal token (low Rank-1 accuracy), the fact that coverage surges to over 80% within the top-3 ranks indicates that the model is suffering from decision ambiguity among a few strong candidates, rather than lacking the requisite knowledge.

F.3 Performance of distilled selector

To provide a rigorous analysis of the selector’s performance, we first define the evaluation metrics utilized in Table A2:

  • •

    Selection Alignment: includes Agree@1, which measures the frequency with which the selector’s top choice matches the teacher’s preferred candidate; Kendall’s τ\tau and Spearman ρ\rho quantify the rank correlation between the distilled scoring and the teacher’s probability distribution.

  • •

    Confidence on selected tokens: compares the probability assigned to the selected token by the base SLM, the LLM (teacher), and the distilled selector (Score).

  • •

    Prediction confidence: measured via entropy, where lower values indicate a more ”peaked” or certain distribution, comparing the teacher’s certainty against the selector’s scoring sharpens.

The results demonstrate that the distilled selector achieves substantial alignment fidelity with teacher preferences across all benchmarks, significantly outperforming the Random baseline (12.5%12.5\%). While performance scales with model capacity, as the 1.5B model reaches over 70%70\% Agree@1 accuracy, the 0.5B variant still maintains strong rank correlations (ρ≈0.50\rho\approx 0.50), proving that even extremely small models can internalize complex ranking hierarchies.

Across diverse tasks ranging from linguistic reasoning (MMLU-Pro) to formal mathematics (AIME25), the selector exhibits robust stability, confirming that the Select to Think paradigm is effective regardless of the underlying student scale. A critical finding lies in the calibration recovery observed in the confidence metrics, particularly for the 1.5B model. The data reveals that the selector frequently identifies tokens where the base SLM probability is low (≈25−30%\approx 25-30\%) but the LLM probability is high (≈60−70%\approx 60-70\%). By elevating the Score probability to over 80−90%80-90\%, the selector effectively “rescues” optimal candidates that were previously underestimated by the student’s original distribution. This demonstrates that S2T does not merely mimic the student’s existing biases, but successfully adopts the teacher’s discriminative logic to overcome the student’s inherent calibration failures.

To gain a deeper understanding of the selector’s behavior, we visualize the distribution of predicted scores against the ground-truth ranks assigned by the teacher in Figure A5. The violin plot reveals a striking “winner-takes-all” characteristic: High fidelity on top-1: The distribution for Rank 1 is heavily skewed towards the top (median ≈\approx 0.9), indicating that the selector consistently assigns high confidence to the teacher’s preferred token. Sharp discrimination: We observe a precipitous drop in scores from Rank 1 to Rank 2, with the median score plunging to near zero. This suggests that the selector does not merely learn a soft correlation; instead, it establishes a sharp decision boundary, effectively suppressing sub-optimal candidates (Ranks 2-8) to eliminate ambiguity. This decisive separation explains why the S2T-Local model achieves high performance even with a small candidate set: it acts as a high-precision filter that decisively isolates the optimal path.

F.4 Extended efficiency analysis

The efficiency analysis in Table A3 underscores the practical viability of our framework, revealing that S2T-Local successfully eliminates the prohibitive latency overhead typically associated with teacher-student collaboration. While standard collaborative methods like SpecReason and LLM-takeover incur significant delays due to real-time teacher intervention, S2T-Local achieves inference latencies nearly identical to that of standard SLM (Greedy) decoding. Specifically, it delivers a consistent ∼75%{\sim}75\% time reduction compared to the LLM-takeover baseline across all benchmarks, notably reducing AIME25 latency from 81.5​s81.5\text{s} to just 21.0​s21.0\text{s}. Crucially, this massive acceleration is achieved without a corresponding reduction in generated token counts, proving that the efficiency gains stem entirely from internalizing the selection logic into the local model rather than simply truncating the reasoning paths. By bypassing the need for expensive online teacher calls, S2T-Local effectively provides a significant performance boost, maintaining the native inference speed of small-scale models while significantly elevating their reasoning accuracy.

Interestingly, as shown in Table A4, the time consumption remains remarkably stable across various trigger rates and KK values (averaging around 10.0s), with only a marginal overhead compared to the SLM greedy baseline (9.3s).

F.5 Ablation on trigger mechanism

Table A5 substantiates that the efficacy of S2T is not dependent on a specific uncertainty measure, confirming the framework’s metric-agnostic robustness. Both Entropy and KL-divergence triggers significantly outperform the Random baseline, which lacks the targeted intervention necessary to resolve student failures. While the choice of metric influences the specific intervention points, S2T consistently leverages these signals to bridge the reasoning gap. This invariance demonstrates that the strength of our approach lies in the selection mechanism itself, rather than in the hyper-parameter tuning of a particular trigger.
